quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-01.title: Disjoint normal subgroups commute
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-01.body:
**(a)** Let $g\in C_G(K)$, $h\in H$. For $k\in K$, $k^{h^{-1}}\in K$ since $K\trianglelefteq H$, so $g$ commutes with $k^{h^{-1}}$; conjugating by $h$, $g^h$ commutes with $k$. Thus $g^h\in C_G(K)$ for all $h\in H$, i.e. $H$ normalizes $C_G(K)$.

**(b)** Let $C=C_G(K)$. By (a), $\bar G=HC$ is a subgroup and $C\trianglelefteq\bar G$ (it is normalized by $H$ and by itself). Since $H\trianglelefteq G$, also $H\trianglelefteq\bar G$. Moreover $H\cap C=C_H(K)=1$. For $h\in H$, $c\in C$, the commutator $[h,c]=h^{-1}(c^{-1}hc)\in H$ and $[h,c]=(h^{-1}c^{-1}h)c\in C$, so $[h,c]\in H\cap C=1$. Hence $H$ centralizes $C_G(K)$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-02.title: Maximal counterexample
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-02.body:
**(a)** Since $Q$ is not prime, there are ideals $A',B'$ with $A'B'\subseteq Q$, $A'\not\subseteq Q$, $B'\not\subseteq Q$. Let $A=A'+Q$, $B=B'+Q$; these are ideals properly containing $Q$, and $AB\subseteq A'B'+A'Q+QB'+QQ\subseteq Q$.

**(b)** Note $Q\ne R$ (as $R\supseteq I^1$). Suppose $Q$ is not prime and take $A,B\supsetneq Q$ with $AB\subseteq Q$ as in (a). By maximality of $Q$, $A\supseteq I^m$ and $B\supseteq I^k$ for some $m,k\ge1$. Then $I^{m+k}=I^mI^k\subseteq AB\subseteq Q$, contradicting the choice of $Q$. So $Q$ is prime.

**(c)** Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of ideals containing no power of $I$. As $I$ is not nilpotent, $0\in\mathcal S$. ACC on ideals is equivalent to every nonempty family of ideals having a maximal member, so $\mathcal S$ has a maximal member $Q$. By (b), $Q$ is prime, and $I\not\subseteq Q$ since $Q\in\mathcal S$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-03.title: Splitting fields and restriction
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-03.body:
**(a)** $E$ and $F$ are splitting fields over $K$ of separable polynomials $f,g\in K[x]$. The subfield of $L$ generated over $K$ by the roots of $f$ and $g$ contains $E$ and $F$, hence equals $L$. So $L$ is the splitting field over $K$ of $\mathrm{lcm}(f,g)$, whose irreducible factors each divide $f$ or $g$ and are therefore separable. Hence $L/K$ is normal and separable, i.e. Galois.

**(b)** Let $T=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$. As $E/K$ is normal, every $t\in T$ maps $E$ onto itself, so restriction gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon T\to G$; similarly $\varphi\colon T\to H$. Then $\psi(t)=(\theta(t),\varphi(t))$ is a homomorphism $T\to G\times H$. If $\psi(t)=1$, then $t$ fixes $E$ and $F$ pointwise; the fixed field of $t$ is a subfield of $L$ containing $E$ and $F$, so it is $L$ and $t=1$. Thus $\psi$ is injective and $T\cong\psi(T)\le G\times H$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-04.title: Characteristic and minimal polynomials
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-04.body:
**(a)** Let $A(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\8&x\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is
$$\varphi(\lambda)=\lambda^2-(x+1)\lambda+(x+16).$$
If $\varphi$ has distinct roots, $A(x)$ is diagonalizable. It has a double root iff the discriminant vanishes: $(x+1)^2=4(x+16)$, i.e. $x^2-2x-63=(x-9)(x+7)=0$. For $x=9$, $\varphi=(\lambda-5)^2$; for $x=-7$, $\varphi=(\lambda+3)^2$. If $A(x)$ were then diagonalizable it would be similar to the scalar matrix $\mu I$, hence equal to $\mu I$; but $A(x)$ has off-diagonal entries $-2,8\ne0$. So $A(x)$ is **not** diagonalizable exactly for $x=9$ and $x=-7$.

**(b)** $J^2=nJ$ (each entry of $J^2$ is $n$), so $J$ satisfies $\lambda(\lambda-n)$, which has distinct roots $0,n$ (for $n\ge1$). Hence $J$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues in $\{0,n\}$, say $J\sim D$ with $b$ entries equal to $n$ and the rest $0$. Comparing traces, $n=\mathrm{tr}\,J=bn$, so $b=1$. Thus
$$J\sim D=\mathrm{diag}(n,0,\dots,0).$$
(Equivalently: $\mathrm{rank}\,J=1$, so $D$ has one nonzero entry, which equals $\mathrm{tr}\,J=n$; the vector $(1,\dots,1)$ is an eigenvector for $n$, and the $(n-1)$-dimensional kernel consists of vectors with coordinate sum $0$.) ∎

**(b)** Let $	heta\colon F[x,y]	o F$ be evaluation at $(\alpha, eta)$; it is surjective, so $J=\ker	heta$ is maximal ($F[x,y]/J\cong F$), and $I\subseteq J$. Conversely, $x\equiv\alpha$ and $y\equiv eta\pmod I$, so for any $h$, $h(x,y)\equiv h(\alpha, eta)\pmod I$. If $h\in J$ then $h\equiv0\pmod I$, i.e. $h\in I$. So $I=J$ is maximal. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-05.title: Dimension count for (a)
quals-wisconsin-algebra-1999f-05.body: For (a) one can also argue: $F[x,y]/(f,g)\cong F[x]/(f)\otimes_FF[y]/(g)$, which has $F$-dimension $\deg f\cdot\deg g>0$; concretely, the monomials $x^iy^j$ with $i<\deg f$, $j<\deg g$ form a basis modulo $I$ (divide by the monic versions of $f$ in $x$ and $g$ in $y$). A nonzero quotient means $I\ne F[x,y]$. For (b), with $\deg f=\deg g=1$ the quotient is $1$-dimensional, spanned by the image of $1$, so $F[x,y]/I\cong F$ is a field and $I$ is maximal. ∎
